title: Whisky and Coffee Pairing | Craft Beer School
desc: How to pair whisky with coffee, from South Indian filter coffee to cold brew and Irish coffee, with the whisky styles that suit each roast.
teaser: Coffee and whisky share roast, sweetness and bitterness. Here is how to pair them without one flattening the other.
standfirst: Coffee and whisky both carry roast, caramel and bitterness. Pair them by intensity, think about roast level and keep the measures small. Then they can show each other off.
sections: Why coffee and whisky get along

Coffee and whisky share a surprising amount. Roasting coffee beans creates caramel, chocolate, nutty and smoky aromas. Charred oak casks give whisky vanilla, caramel and toast. Both have bitterness, both have sweetness and both have a long finish.

That overlap is why the pairing works. It is also why it can go wrong: two strong, roasty drinks can drown each other. The aim is to match intensity and let one bring out something in the other.
Match roast level to whisky style

Roast level is the main guide.

  • Light roast coffee is bright, fruity and acidic. It suits light, fruity whiskies from ex-bourbon casks.
  • Medium roast has caramel and chocolate. It suits bourbon and many blended Scotches.
  • Dark roast is bitter, smoky and heavy. It can stand up to sherry cask whiskies and peated malts.

India grows a lot of coffee, mainly in Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu, in regions such as Chikmagalur and Coorg. Single estate beans from these regions are easy to find and make a good starting point for experiments.
South Indian filter coffee and whisky

Filter coffee, brewed in a steel filter, often with chicory, then served with hot milk and sugar, is strong, sweet and slightly bitter. That makes it a challenging partner for whisky. The milk and sugar soften it, but chicory adds a roasted bitterness of its own.

A bourbon or a sherried blend works best alongside. Vanilla and dried fruit pick up the caramel in the coffee and its sweetness. Serve them side by side rather than mixed: a small cup of filter coffee, a 15 ml pour of whisky and a glass of water. Taste the coffee first, then the whisky. Notice how each changes the other.
Irish coffee floats the cream, never stirs it

Irish coffee is the best known whisky and coffee drink: hot coffee, Irish whiskey and brown sugar, topped with lightly whipped cream floated on top. The cream is not stirred in. You drink the hot coffee through the cool cream.

A simple home version uses 30 ml of whiskey, 120 ml of strong hot coffee, a teaspoon of brown sugar or jaggery and a spoon of lightly whipped cream poured over the back of a spoon. A light, smooth Irish whiskey suits it best. Peated or heavily sherried whiskies tend to clash with the cream.

Cold brew coffee, steeped in cold water for many hours, is smoother and less acidic than hot coffee. In Indian summers it is a better partner for whisky than hot coffee. A splash of whisky in cold brew over ice, with a little milk or condensed milk if you like it sweet, makes a gentle, refreshing drink.

Bourbon is the classic choice here because its vanilla and caramel echo the coffee. Keep the whisky to around 30 ml per glass.
Watch the caffeine and the clock

Mixing alcohol with caffeine is common, but caffeine can make you feel more alert than you are. It does not reduce the effect of alcohol or make it safer to drive. If you are pairing whisky and coffee at the end of a meal, keep pours small and count the whisky as you normally would.

Late evening coffee can also keep you awake. Decaffeinated beans work well for pairing and lose little flavour. Our guide to whisky and Indian food covers the rest of the meal.
Desserts bring coffee and whisky together

Coffee and whisky also meet on the dessert plate. A tiramisu, a coffee mousse or an affogato, vanilla ice cream with a shot of hot espresso poured over it, all pair well with a small pour of bourbon or a sherried malt alongside. Some cooks add a spoonful of whisky to the espresso for an affogato.

Chocolate brings a third partner into the mix. Dark chocolate, coffee and a sherry cask whisky share roast and dried fruit notes, so they tend to agree. Milk chocolate suits lighter, honeyed whiskies better. Keep any whisky in desserts away from children and tell guests it is there.
Run a coffee and whisky flight

Brew two coffees, one light roast and one dark. Pour two whiskies, one light and fruity, one rich or sherried, about 15 ml each. Taste each coffee with each whisky, side by side rather than mixed. Note which pairing lifts both.

Most people find the light roast and light whisky match brightly, while the dark roast and sherried whisky make a deep, dessert like pairing. Writing down what you taste builds the sensory vocabulary that carries across coffee, whisky and beer. Start with your usual morning coffee and one whisky after dinner this weekend.
faqs: What whisky goes best with coffee?
Bourbon and smooth blends suit most coffee. Light fruity whiskies suit light roasts. Sherried or peated whiskies can match dark roasts.
How do you make Irish coffee?
Mix hot coffee with Irish whiskey and brown sugar, then float lightly whipped cream on top without stirring it in.
Does coffee sober you up after whisky?
No. Caffeine can make you feel more alert, but it does not reduce the effect of alcohol or make it safe to drive.
Can I add whisky to cold brew?
Yes. Around 30 ml of bourbon or a smooth blend in cold brew over ice makes a refreshing drink for hot weather.
